[Beyond the Scrum Guide] = practical steps and examples for the objective "perform a Sprint Planning", which the Guide does not spell out. [Old wording] = a term from the 2017 Guide that a question may still use.

toc.title: What the Guide Does Not Prescribe
Inspect and Adapt in Sprint Planning (CSM 1.7)
Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1Purpose, Participants and Timebox

Item What the Guide says
Purpose Sprint Planning initiates the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed for the Sprint
Who creates the plan "This resulting plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team"
Preparation "The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal"
Others "The Scrum Team may also invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice"
Timebox A maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints the event is usually shorter
Output The Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected and the plan for delivering them, together called the Sprint Backlog
Exam angle

Sprint Planning is for the whole Scrum Team (Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master). The plan is not handed down by the Product Owner, the Scrum Master or a manager, and the Developers are not told how to do the work.

2The Three Topics

Topic One: Why is this Sprint valuable?

  • The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint.
  • The whole Scrum Team collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders.
  • "The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning."

Topic Two: What can be Done this Sprint?

  • "Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint."
  • The Scrum Team may refine these items during the process, "which increases understanding and confidence."
  • Selecting how much can be completed may be challenging. The more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts.

Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?

  • For each selected item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done.
  • "This is often done by decomposing Product Backlog items into smaller work items of one day or less."
  • "How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value."
Topic Question Who leads Result
One Why is this Sprint valuable? Product Owner proposes; the whole Scrum Team defines the goal The Sprint Goal
Two What can be Done this Sprint? Developers select, in discussion with the Product Owner The selected Product Backlog items
Three How will the chosen work get done? The Developers The plan (decomposed work)
Old wording

The 2017 Guide had two topics, "What can be done this Sprint?" and "How will the chosen work get done?", and described the Sprint Backlog as "a forecast by the Development Team about what functionality will be in the next Increment". The 2020 Guide adds Topic One: Why and describes the Sprint Backlog as "a plan by and for the Developers". In 2017 the Development Team "works to forecast the functionality"; in 2020 the Developers "select" items and gain confidence in their "forecasts".

3What the Guide Does Not Prescribe

Not in the Guide What to answer
A technique for sizing or forecasting (story points, hours, velocity) The Developers choose how they forecast: past performance, capacity and the Definition of Done guide confidence. "Relative story points" are absent from the Guide
A format for Product Backlog items (user stories) The Product Backlog item's attributes "often vary with the domain of work"
Approval of the Sprint Backlog by a manager or the Scrum Master The plan belongs to the Developers
A required number of items or hours The Developers decide how much they can do

Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are "deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event" (Topic 10).

4Performing a Sprint Planning (CSM 1.8)Beyond the Guide

The objective is practised in class. This checklist follows the Guide's three topics and adds the usual practical steps.

Phase What to do Who
Before The Product Backlog is ordered and the top items are refined; the Product Owner thinks through the value the Sprint could bring and the Product Goal; the team checks its capacity (holidays, availability) and recalls its past performance and Definition of Done; time and place are fixed Product Owner, Developers, Scrum Master
Open State the Product Goal and the time available; remind the team of the timebox Scrum Master, Product Owner
Topic One: Why The Product Owner proposes the value; the team writes a single, coherent Sprint Goal Whole Scrum Team
Topic Two: What Starting from the top of the Product Backlog, the Developers discuss items with the Product Owner, refine where needed, and select what they are confident they can Done in the Sprint Developers with the Product Owner
Topic Three: How The Developers decompose the selected items, think through the Definition of Done, dependencies and the first days of work; unrealistic parts are revisited Developers
Check Is the plan realistic and still serving the Sprint Goal? Is the Sprint Goal finalized? Is the Sprint Backlog visible to everyone? Whole Scrum Team
Close End within the timebox; the Sprint starts immediately Scrum Master ensures

4.1 What a good Sprint Goal looks like Beyond the Guide

The Guide: the Sprint Goal is "the single objective for the Sprint", it gives flexibility in the exact work, and "creates coherence and focus, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives".

Good Weak
One objective that explains why the Sprint is valuable: "Customers can pay with a saved card" A list of items: "Do items 12, 14, 17 and 19"
States an outcome, with flexibility about which items achieve it A layer or activity with no value: "Finish the back end"
Understandable by stakeholders Everything in the Sprint: "Complete the Sprint Backlog"

5Roles in Sprint Planning

Who Role
Product Owner Ensures attendees are prepared; proposes how the product could increase its value; discusses items with the Developers; helps shape the Sprint Goal
Developers Select the items; forecast what they can do; plan how; own the resulting plan
Scrum Master A member of the Scrum Team; ensures the event takes place and is positive, productive and within the timebox; helps the team understand Scrum
Others invited Give advice (for example an expert); they do not decide

6Inspect and Adapt in Sprint Planning (CSM 1.7)Beyond the Guide

The Guide says every event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt, and it names what is inspected for the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. It names nothing for Sprint Planning, so these examples are practice for the objective.

Inspect Adapt Transparency
The Product Backlog and the Product Goal; past performance; capacity; the Definition of Done Select a realistic set of items and set a Sprint Goal; refine or split items that do not fit The Sprint Goal and the Sprint Backlog make the plan visible to the whole team and to stakeholders

7Common ProblemsBeyond the Guide

Problem Better practice
No Sprint Goal, or a list of tasks Define one objective; finalize it before the end of Planning
The Product Owner assigns the work or the load Developers select and decide how much
Items too big to finish in a Sprint Refine or split; only items that can be Done in a Sprint are ready
Planning exceeds the timebox Prepare the Product Backlog beforehand; the Scrum Master keeps the timebox
The plan ignores the Definition of Done Plan the work needed to meet it for each item
Overcommitment Use past performance and capacity; plan for the first days in detail

8Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. Three topics: why (Sprint Goal), what (selected items), how (plan). The "why" is new in 2020.
  2. The Sprint Goal is created in Sprint Planning and finalized before the end of it.
  3. The Developers select the items, in discussion with the Product Owner. The Product Owner does not assign them.
  4. The Developers decide how. No one else, including the Product Owner and the Scrum Master.
  5. The whole Scrum Team creates the plan. It is not the Product Owner's plan or a manager's.
  6. Maximum eight hours for a one-month Sprint, shorter for shorter Sprints; the Scrum Master ensures the timebox is kept.
  7. Others may be invited for advice, not to decide.
  8. Sprint Backlog = Sprint Goal + selected items + plan. The 2017 "forecast" wording is old.
  9. Items ready for selection can be Done within one Sprint. Large vague items should be refined first.
  10. No prescribed estimation technique. Story points, velocity and hours belong to team choice.
  11. Work items of one day or less are "often" used for the plan, not a rule.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The Product Owner says that the Sprint needs no Sprint Goal because the Product Backlog items are clear. What should the Scrum Master advise?

  • AAgree: the Sprint Goal is optional when the Product Backlog items are clear and ordered, because the items already show what the Sprint is for
  • BThe Scrum Team should define a Sprint Goal that explains why the Sprint is valuable and finalize it before Planning ends
  • CLet the Developers write the Sprint Goal after the Sprint starts, once they know how the work is going
  • DAsk the stakeholders to provide the Sprint Goal after the Sprint Review, when they have seen the Increment
Show the answer

Answer: B. Topic One of Sprint Planning is "Why is this Sprint valuable?", and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal, which must be finalized before the end of Sprint Planning. It is part of the Sprint Backlog and gives the Sprint coherence and focus.

S2In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner hands the Developers a list of items and says they must all be done in this Sprint. What is the best response?

  • AThe Developers select the items, through discussion with the Product Owner, based on what they can do
  • BThe Scrum Master edits the list
  • CThe stakeholders vote on the list
  • DThe Developers accept, because the Product Owner decides the Sprint's work
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Developers select items from the Product Backlog for the Sprint through discussion with the Product Owner, using their knowledge of past performance, capacity and the Definition of Done. The Product Owner does not assign the load.

S3The Developers have only recently formed and have no data about past performance. What helps them most in selecting items?

  • AUse their upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done, select a modest set and refine items to build confidence
  • BSelect everything the Product Owner asks for, since without any data the Developers cannot judge what would be too much for them
  • CAsk the Scrum Master to choose the items, because the Scrum Master can see the whole picture of the team
  • DSkip Topic Two and begin the Sprint with the Sprint Goal only, adding items as the Developers finish
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Guide says that the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done, the more confident they are in their forecasts, and that refining items during Planning increases understanding and confidence. A new team uses what it has and inspects the result.

S4One top-ordered item is far too large to be finished in a Sprint. What should the Scrum Team do in Sprint Planning?

  • ASelect it anyway
  • BLeave it out and never refine it
  • CRefine or split it, so that part of it can be Done within the Sprint
  • DAsk the Scrum Master to reduce its size
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Scrum Team may refine items during Sprint Planning, and items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection. Splitting lets the team take the part that fits and keep the rest in the Product Backlog.

S5A manager asks to approve the Sprint Backlog's design details before the Sprint starts. What is the best response?

  • AAgree, because managers are accountable for the quality of the work that their staff deliver to the customers
  • BExplain that how Product Backlog items become Increments is at the sole discretion of the Developers
  • CAsk the Product Owner to approve the design instead, since the Product Owner is accountable for the value
  • DAsk the Scrum Master to approve the design instead, since the Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Developers plan the work and no one else tells them how to turn items into Increments. The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. The manager can inspect the plan, which is visible, and see the results at the Sprint Review.

S6Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint has reached eight hours without finishing. What should the Scrum Master do?

  • ARemind the team that eight hours is the maximum, help it conclude with what it has, and prepare better next time
  • BContinue until the plan is complete, even into the next day, because an incomplete plan puts the whole Sprint at risk
  • CAsk the Product Owner to finish the plan alone after the meeting and send it to the Developers for approval
  • DCancel the Sprint and schedule a new Sprint Planning with a longer timebox so that the plan can be completed
Show the answer

Answer: A. Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the Scrum Master ensures events are kept within the timebox. Better preparation of the Product Backlog and a smaller plan are the adaptation. Extending the event or handing the plan to one person is not an option.

S7The Developers want a security expert, who is not on the Scrum Team, to advise on a risky item during Sprint Planning. What does the Guide say?

  • AExperts are not allowed, because Sprint Planning is only for the Product Owner, the Developers and the Scrum Master
  • BThe expert must replace one of the Developers for the Sprint, because only Scrum Team members may attend
  • CThe expert decides which items go into the Sprint, since the expert knows the risk better than the team
  • DThe Scrum Team may invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Scrum Team may invite others to attend Sprint Planning to give advice. The expert advises and does not become a member of the team or decide the plan.

S8The Product Owner arrives at Sprint Planning without having thought about what the Sprint should achieve, and the Product Backlog is in disorder. How can the Scrum Master best help?

  • AChoose the Sprint Goal for the Product Owner, since the Scrum Master has seen the stakeholders' needs
  • BCancel the Sprint Planning and reschedule it for the following week, once the Product Owner is better prepared and the Product Backlog is in order again
  • CHelp the Product Owner with techniques to prepare so that attendees can discuss the most important items and the Product Goal
  • DAsk the Developers to order the Product Backlog during the meeting, because they know the work best
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal. The Scrum Master helps find techniques for Product Backlog management. Choosing for the Product Owner or handing the order to the Developers undermines the Product Owner's accountability.

S9Which of these is the best Sprint Goal?

  • AComplete items 12, 14, 17 and 19
  • BFinish the back end of the checkout
  • CFix all bugs reported by testers
  • DCustomers can check out using a saved payment method
Show the answer

Answer: D. A Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint, it explains why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders and it allows flexibility in the exact work needed. A list of items, a technical layer or an open-ended activity does not communicate value.

S10At the end of Sprint Planning, what does the Sprint Backlog consist of?

  • AThe Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, together with an estimate of the effort and the person responsible for each item
  • BThe plan for the Developers' first day of work only, with a task list for each Developer
  • CThe Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, and the plan for delivering them
  • DThe Product Backlog and the Sprint Goal, with the order that the Product Owner has set for the items
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Sprint Goal, the items selected for the Sprint and the plan for delivering them are together referred to as the Sprint Backlog.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the purpose of Sprint Planning?

Show the answer

To initiate the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed. The plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team.

R2What are the three topics of Sprint Planning?

Show the answer

Why is this Sprint valuable? What can be Done this Sprint? How will the chosen work get done?

R3Who proposes the value in Topic One?

Show the answer

The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility; the whole Scrum Team defines the Sprint Goal.

R4When must the Sprint Goal be finalized?

Show the answer

Before the end of Sprint Planning.

R5Who selects the items for the Sprint?

Show the answer

The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner.

R6What helps the Developers gain confidence in their forecasts?

Show the answer

Knowing their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done.

R7Who decides how the work gets done?

Show the answer

The Developers, at their sole discretion.

R8Into what size is work often decomposed?

Show the answer

Smaller work items of one day or less.

R9What is the Sprint Backlog?

Show the answer

The Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, and the plan for delivering them.

R10What is the maximum timebox of Sprint Planning?

Show the answer

Eight hours for a one-month Sprint; usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

R11What must the Product Owner ensure before Sprint Planning?

Show the answer

That attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal.

R12Who may attend Sprint Planning besides the Scrum Team?

Show the answer

Other people invited by the Scrum Team to provide advice.

R13How did the 2017 Guide describe Sprint Planning's topics?

Show the answer

Two topics (what, how) instead of three; the Sprint Backlog was described as a forecast.

R14Name three signs of a good Sprint Goal.

Show the answer

One objective; explains why the Sprint is valuable; flexible about the exact work; coherent and focusing; understood by stakeholders.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Purpose Initiates the Sprint by laying out the work; plan created by the whole Scrum Team
Attendees Scrum Team; others may be invited for advice
Timebox Max 8 hours for a one-month Sprint; shorter for shorter Sprints
Topic One Why: Product Owner proposes value; team defines the Sprint Goal (finalized before the end)
Topic Two What: Developers select items with the Product Owner; use past performance, capacity, Definition of Done
Topic Three How: Developers plan the work; often items of one day or less; sole discretion
Output Sprint Backlog = Sprint Goal + selected items + plan
Product Owner ensures Attendees prepared on the most important items and the Product Goal
Not prescribed Story points, velocity, user stories
Old wording Two topics, "forecast", Development Team (2017)
